**1 G** é a aceleração da gravidade, a q: **1 G** is the acceleration of gravity, what the body feels standing on the ground. When the airplane accelerates, brakes or turns, the body comes to weigh **several times its own weight**: at **9 G**, a 70 kg person weighs the equivalent of **630 kg**. The blood, the organs and the head get heavier too.
**Altitude de cabine** é a pressão dentr: **Cabin altitude** is the pressure inside the cabin expressed as the equivalent altitude above sea level. In cruise at 38,000 ft, the body is not at 38,000 ft: it is at the altitude that the cabin pressure represents.
**Caças e aviões acrobáticos chegam a 9: **Fighters and aerobatic airplanes reach 9 G**, and an aircraft carrier catapult takes the airplane to more than **250 km/h in less than 2 seconds**. According to the FAA, civil pilots can also be **surprised by high G** in a tight turn or when recovering from an unusual attitude, and they almost never have an anti-G suit.
**Hiperventilar** é respirar além do nec: **Hyperventilating** is breathing more than necessary and blowing off too much **carbon dioxide**. Anxiety, pain, stress and altitude itself can trigger it. The dizziness and tingling resemble hypoxia, but the mechanism is different.
**Hipotermia** é a temperatura central d: **Hypothermia** is a core temperature of **35 °C or less**. At around **34 °C**, the brain already works more slowly. Shivering, the main defense, **decreases around 32 °C and stops near 30 °C**. Below that, the heart slows and the risk of **arrhythmia** soars.
**Hipóxia** é a falta de oxigênio nos te: **Hypoxia** is a lack of oxygen in the tissues, from insufficient supply or use. Altitude is only one of the causes: the failure can happen at any step between the air and the cell. That is why aerospace medicine divides it into **four mechanisms**, which can add up.
**Impacto** é uma aceleração de **fração: **Impact** is an acceleration lasting a **fraction of a second**: the jolt of a hard landing, of an accident or of leaving an ejection seat. It differs from the sustained G of turns, which lasts seconds (See M1V7). In an impact, blood has no time to shift; what suffers is the **structure of the body**: bones, ligaments and organs that keep moving when the seat has already stopped.
**Lei de Boyle:** com a temperatura cons: **Boyle's law:** at constant temperature, pressure and volume move in opposite directions (P₁V₁ = P₂V₂). Less pressure, more volume. That is why a sealed bag puffs up during the climb, and air trapped in the body's cavities does the same.
**Lei de Charles:** com a pressão consta: **Charles's law:** at constant pressure, volume follows absolute temperature; in a rigid container, it is the pressure that follows (**Gay-Lussac**). Because the body regulates its own temperature, the effect shows up in equipment: in the cold, the **oxygen cylinder** reads lower pressure without having lost any gas.
**Lei de Dalton:** a pressão total do ar: **Dalton's law:** the total pressure of air is the sum of the pressures of each gas. Oxygen is still 20.95% of dry air, but its **partial pressure** falls along with total pressure, and that is what pushes oxygen into the blood. Once humidified in the airways, inspired oxygen equals 0.2095 × (PB − 47): **149 mmHg at sea level, 108 mmHg at 8,000 ft and 70 mmHg at 18,000 ft**. This gives rise to **hypoxic hypoxia** and the need for supplemental oxygen.
**Lei de Henry:** a quantidade de gás di: **Henry's law:** the amount of gas dissolved in a liquid follows that gas's pressure. When pressure falls, tissues become **supersaturated with nitrogen**, which tends to come out as bubbles: this is the mechanism of **decompression sickness** (See M1V3). The risk grows with rapid decompressions and after diving with compressed gas.
**Pressurizar não dispensa o oxigênio.**: **Pressurization does not replace oxygen.** A failure or a decompression is always possible, which is why supplemental oxygen remains on board (See M1V3).

A **ICRP**, comissão internacional de pr: The **ICRP**, the international commission on radiological protection, recommends for exposed workers an effective dose of **20 mSv per year, averaged over 5 years**, without exceeding **50 mSv in any single year**; the **FAA** adopts the same values. For the general public, the limit is **1 mSv per year**. These numbers do not separate safe from dangerous: they are the **ceiling of the acceptable**. Medical exams do not count toward it. The limits serve two purposes: avoiding **tissue reactions**, which only appear above a threshold, and keeping the risk of **cancer**, which has no threshold, low. For the **lens of the eye**, the ICRP lowered the estimated **cataract** threshold to about **0.5 Gy** and the occupational eye limit from 150 to **20 mSv per year**, averaged over 5 years; flight doses are far below that.
A **atmosfera** é a camada de gases que: The **atmosphere** is the layer of gases surrounding the Earth. Dry air is **78.08% nitrogen**, **20.95% oxygen**, 0.93% argon and about 0.04% carbon dioxide, plus traces of other gases. Water vapor varies with the weather. Within the flight range, this recipe barely changes.
A **centrífuga humana** gira uma cabine: The **human centrifuge** spins a cabin on a long arm and creates **sustained G**, safely, with doctors monitoring the pilot by video and electrocardiogram. Under the **NATO** standard, training uses the aircraft's G, usually **up to 9 G**, with a rapid onset of at least **3 G per second**, and each person learns to recognize **their own signs** of impending G-LOC and to perform the right maneuver.
A **curva de dissociação da oxi-hemoglob: The **oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve** explains the danger: at first, saturation holds up; past a certain point, each further drop in pressure brings saturation down faster and faster. Altitude, exposure time, breathing and disease change this response. Finding out at which of the four steps oxygen failed is the first step to correcting it.
A **manobra anti-G** é ativa. O piloto *: The **anti-G straining maneuver** is active. The pilot **forcefully tenses the legs, abdomen and arms** and strains to exhale against a **closed glottis** for **3 to 4 seconds**, followed by a **quick inhalation**, repeating the cycle. Pressure in the chest rises and pushes blood toward the head. Well trained, it provided about **3 G** of protection; tensing alone, about **2 G**. It is tiring, and the FAA warns: **do not perform it at full strength at 1 G**, to avoid injury.
The **brace position** also protects. In **17 sled tests**, the FAA found that resting **the hands and head on the seatback in front** only helped if the seatback was locked; with a seatback that **breaks over** or **absorbs energy**, it made the head strike worse. With the **hands down, next to the legs**, the risk to the **head and neck** fell significantly for all seatbacks, and the FAA's official recommendation changed.
A **umidade relativa** mostra quanto do: **Relative humidity** shows how much of the vapor possible at that temperature is already in the air. Heated without gaining vapor, air becomes relatively drier. The **dew point** is the temperature at which air, as it cools, becomes saturated. The closer the temperature is to it, the closer the air is to saturation, which does not guarantee fog.
A **vibração de corpo inteiro** chega pe: **Whole-body vibration** arrives through the **seat**, the backrest and the floor, and is measured as **acceleration**, in **meters per second squared (m/s²)**. The body does not react equally to all frequencies. On the **vertical** axis, from feet to head, the greatest sensitivity is between **4 and 8 Hz**, the range of the body's main **resonance**, in which it amplifies the movement; on the lateral axis, between **1 and 2 Hz**.
A **visão noturna** é das mais sensíveis: **Night vision** is among the most sensitive and can worsen even at moderate altitudes. Then recent memory, reasoning and fine movements suffer. In chamber training, each person learns to recognize their own set of symptoms: the **individual hypoxia signature**.
A **água fria** é o cenário mais traiçoe: **Cold water** is the most treacherous setting, and the rule is **1-10-1**. In the **first minute**, **cold shock** causes gasping: the danger is **inhaling water**, so controlling breathing comes before anything else. Then there are about **10 minutes of useful movement** before the muscles fail. Hypothermia takes **at least half an hour** and, by about **1 hour**, leads to unconsciousness. **Most deaths happen at the start, not from hypothermia.**
A 115 dB(A), a NR-15 permite só 7 minuto: At 115 dB(A), NR-15 allows only 7 minutes; above that, no one may stay without adequate protection.
A 1ª classe vale 12 meses. Cai para 6 me: 1st class is valid for 12 months. It drops to 6 months in public transport from age 60, or from age 40 for a single pilot carrying passengers.
A 2,8 ATA (18 m de mar), a bolha encolhe: At 2.8 ATA (18 m of seawater), the bubble shrinks by Boyle's law and the nitrogen gradient rises from 142 to 2,086 mmHg with pure oxygen.
A 35.000 ft, o tempo de consciência útil: At 35,000 ft, the time of useful consciousness is about 30 seconds to 1 minute.
A 35.000 ft, sem oxigênio, a consciência: At 35,000 ft, without oxygen, useful consciousness lasts from 30 seconds to 1 minute.
A 3ª classe (controle de tráfego aéreo): 3rd class (air traffic control) is not governed by ANAC.
A 40.000 ft o oxigênio puro inspirado fi: At 40,000 ft, inspired pure oxygen is close to 93 mmHg, below the 149 mmHg of air at sea level; positive pressure makes up the difference.
A 85 dB(A) são 8 horas; a cada 5 dB o te: At 85 dB(A) it is 8 hours; for every 5 dB the time falls roughly by half: 90 dB(A), 4 hours; 100 dB(A), 1 hour.
A Classe 2 exige ouvir a voz de conversa: Class 2 requires hearing a conversational voice at 2 m, back turned.
A FAA exige 3 meses ou mais na mesma dos: The FAA requires 3 months or more on the same dose, with no side effects.
A FAA não exige certificado médico de co: The FAA does not require a medical certificate for flight attendants.
A FAA pede ao menos 12 horas; com parada: The FAA asks for at least 12 hours; with a decompression stop, or to fly above 8,000 ft, 24 hours.
A Gravidade, Esta Grande Escultora: A Gravidade, Esta Grande Escultora (Gravity, This Great Sculptor)
A IA indicou que o documento não pôde se: The AI indicated that the document could not be read reliably. Check it by hand.
A ICAO estabelece os padrões internacion: ICAO sets international standards, including medical requirements.
A Organização da Aviação Civil Internaci: The International Civil Aviation Organization begins operating and creates international medical standards for crew members.
A Primeira Guerra e o médico de voo: World War I and the flight surgeon
A Segunda Guerra e o limite humano: World War II and the human limit
A altitude de cabine de um avião comerci: The cabin altitude of a commercial airplane is usually up to 8,000 ft, about 2,400 m.
A altitude-densidade fica acima de 5.000: Density altitude is above 5,000 ft, and the engine, propeller and wing perform less well.
A atmosfera da nave, os trajes espaciais: The spacecraft's atmosphere, space suits and prebreathing before spacewalks.
A atmosfera padrão, altitude por altitud: The standard atmosphere, altitude by altitude
A atmosfera se organiza em camadas. A **: The atmosphere is organized in layers. The **troposphere**, where we live and fly, holds almost all the water vapor, the clouds and the weather. In it, air cools with height up to the **tropopause**, whose altitude varies with latitude and season.
A atmosfera vista da órbita: a faixa azu: The atmosphere seen from orbit: the thin blue band on the horizon holds almost all of the planet's air.
A audiometria mostra o efeito acumulado;: Audiometry shows the cumulative effect; damage usually starts at the high frequencies.
A audição faz parte do **exame para o ce: Hearing is part of the **medical certificate exam**. The **FAA** accepts hearing a **conversational voice** at about **2 meters**, with the back to the examiner, or an **audiometry** within limits by frequency. **ANAC** requires **audiometry from 250 to 8,000 Hz**, without a hearing aid; for 2nd and 4th class, it accepts the **voice test at 2 meters**, and for 1st class the ear exam is done by an **otolaryngologist**. The clinical evaluation of the ear is in another flight (See M2V3).
A aurora nasce das partículas do Sol que: The aurora is born from particles from the Sun that the magnetic field channels toward the poles, the same regions where the flight dose is highest.
A avaliação é feita em uso do remédio; o: The evaluation is done while on the medication; the RBAC requires the psychiatrist's opinion (67.75(c)).
A barba aumenta a pressão positiva na má: A beard increases positive pressure in the mask.
A barba pode impedir a vedação da máscar: A beard can prevent the mask from sealing and reduce the oxygen received.
A biometria funciona no app instalado no: Biometrics works in the app installed on the phone (Face ID, Touch ID or fingerprint). In the browser, continue without an account for now.
A borda da atmosfera: as moléculas estão: The edge of the atmosphere: molecules are so far apart that they gradually escape into space.
A bordo, o nível depende da aeronave. Pe: On board, the level depends on the aircraft. According to **FAA** data, the cabin of a **transport jet** is between **60 and 88 dB**; the cockpit of a **small single-engine airplane**, between **70 and 90**; that of a **single-rotor helicopter**, between **80 and 102**. Near a **jet engine**, on the ramp, sound ranges from **130 to 160 dB**. For comparison, conversation is between 60 and 65 dB. In single-engine and helicopter cockpits, the top of the range exceeds **85 dB(A)**, the level at which the safe time per day starts to shrink (See M1V6 - III).
A cabine apresenta necessariamente a mes: The cabin necessarily has the same temperature as the outside air.
A cabine de helicóptero de rotor único v: A single-rotor helicopter cockpit ranges from 80 to 102 dB; a single-engine cockpit, from 70 to 90; a transport jet cabin, from 60 to 88.
A cabine ficou entre 70 e 79 dB(A), mas: The cockpit was between 70 and 79 dB(A), but the open headset delivered 77 to 89 dB(A) to the ear; circumaural and ANR headsets kept it up to 80 dB(A).
The cabin works like a rigid balloon. Each airplane withstands a maximum difference between the pressure inside and outside: the **differential pressure**, shown on a gauge. Some aircraft have **relief valves** that protect the structure when this difference goes beyond the limit. If the structure or the system fails, the cabin climbs, and the body is exposed to the real altitude (See M1V3 - I).
A cabine perde pressão em minutos, sem r: The cabin loses pressure over minutes, without noise.
A cabine perde pressão mais rápido do qu: The cabin loses pressure faster than the lungs can empty.
A cabine é um balão sob pressão: The cabin is a balloon under pressure
A camada mais fria da atmosfera, com cer: The coldest layer of the atmosphere, about −86 °C at the top. It is where most meteors burn up. Too high for airplanes and too low for satellites.
A cardiopatia congênita teve cura cirúrg: Was the congenital heart disease unquestionably cured by surgery?
A carga que passa da pelve para a coluna: The load passing from the pelvis to the lumbar spine may not exceed 1,500 lb, about 680 kg-force, to prevent a compression fracture.
A cerca de 18 a 19 km, a pressão é tão b: At about 18 to 19 km, pressure is so low that water boils at 37 °C.
A cineangiocoronariografia após o infart: Was the coronary angiography after the infarction satisfactory?
A cineangiocoronariografia após o proced: Was the coronary angiography after the procedure satisfactory?
A cintilografia após o procedimento foi: Was the scintigraphy after the procedure satisfactory?
A cintilografia miocárdica após o infart: Was the myocardial scintigraphy after the infarction satisfactory?
A colisão de dois Boeing 747 em Tenerife: The collision of two Boeing 747s at Tenerife kills 583 people. The response is crew resource management (CRM) training, adopted from 1981 onward.
A coluna também sente. Num estudo com **: The spine feels it too. In a study of **six helicopters**, the estimated dose for an 8-hour day, the **A(8)**, was between **0.32 and 0.51 m/s²**, in the range where health risk starts to be considered, in a group with a **high incidence of low back pain**. **Posture** is one of the main factors, especially in the helicopter, and ordinary **cushions** can even **amplify** the 4 to 8 Hz range (See M2V12).
A comida é a última prioridade: dá para: Food is the last priority: you can live about 30 days without it.
A conduta não espera: **máscara, oxigêni: The response does not wait: **mask, 100% oxygen, emergency descent and landing** as soon as possible, with the painful joint kept still. **Even if symptoms disappear during descent, the person needs a medical evaluation**, breathing oxygen. If they persist, treatment is in the **hyperbaric chamber** (See M1V3 - IV). And a warning: **100% oxygen during flight does not prevent the disease** if there was no prebreathing before takeoff.
A conduta é a mesma do tempo de consciên: The response is the same as for time of useful consciousness (See M2V1 - III): **when hypoxia is suspected, restore oxygen immediately**, without waiting for late signs.
A conversa fica entre 500 e 3.000 Hz; a: Conversation lies between 500 and 3,000 Hz; the loss begins near 4,000 Hz and only audiometry shows it.
A curva A pesa as frequências como o ouv: The A curve weights frequencies the way the ear perceives them; NR-15 requires measuring in dB(A), close to the ear.
A câmara **hiperbárica** é o tratamento: The **hyperbaric** chamber is the treatment for decompression sickness. The most used is **US Navy Table 6**: **2.8 atmospheres, the equivalent of 18 meters of seawater, breathing 100% oxygen**. The pressure shrinks the bubble to about **one third of its volume** (Boyle's law), and pure oxygen clears the nitrogen out of the way. The chamber also has effects on the body: the most frequent is **ear barotrauma**, when pressure does not equalize, which can **rupture the eardrum**; rarely, oxygen under pressure causes a **seizure**, which stops when it is removed; and the **myopia** that appears with the sessions usually regresses in **6 to 8 weeks**.
A câmara **hipobárica** ensina sem risco: The **hypobaric** chamber teaches without the risk of flight. In a one-day course, the student goes through a **rapid decompression from 8,000 to 18,000 ft** and then **hypoxia at 25,000 ft**, to recognize their own symptoms under supervision. The training is recommended for all pilots (See M3V3). The training also takes a toll on the body: in a study of **1,627 students**, **5.6%** had some adverse effect; the most common was **barotrauma of the ear and sinuses** (69% of these cases), followed by respiratory problems and **decompression sickness**. The authors recommend **prebreathing oxygen for 45 minutes** and climbing at most **3,000 ft per minute**.
A depressão tratada com antidepressivo t: Depression treated with an antidepressant has its own rule just below.
A direção muda tudo. **De frente ou de c: Direction changes everything. **Facing forward or backward**, with the body supported by the seatback or the belts, the load spreads across the trunk and the high-risk limit reaches **46 G**. **Along the spine**, from top to bottom, the same level of risk appears at about **23 G**, because the **vertebrae** take the load one on top of the other. In +Z, **high** risk corresponds to a **50%** chance of **spinal fracture**; **moderate**, to **5%**; **low**, to **0.5%**.
A doença tem várias faces. A mais comum: The disease has several faces. The most common is **deep pain in the large joints**, which worsens with movement. The skin may itch and become **mottled**. In the nerves, **numbness, burning and tingling** appear. In the chest, the **chokes** bring burning pain, dry cough and shortness of breath, and **can kill without treatment**. In the **central nervous system**, confusion, visual changes, seizures, weakness and loss of consciousness appear.
A doença tratada está controlada com o r: Is the treated condition controlled with the medication?
A doença tratada não está controlada com: The treated condition is not controlled with the current medication.
A dose cresce com o tempo no ar, a altit: The dose grows with time in the air, altitude and latitude: New York–Tokyo, long, high and near the pole, exceeds 55 µSv.
A dose no corpo inteiro se mede em **sie: Whole-body dose is measured in **sieverts (Sv)**, as the **effective dose**: it weights the type of radiation and the sensitivity of each organ. Flight doses are small, so the **millisievert (mSv)**, one thousandth, and the **microsievert (µSv)**, one millionth, are used. For reference, in the US natural radiation adds up to an average of **3.11 mSv per year**; almost three quarters come from **radon**, a gas from the ground, and the cosmic part is **0.33 mSv**. In the effective dose, the most sensitive organs weigh more: **bone marrow, colon, lung, stomach and breast** have the greatest weight, followed by the **gonads**; skin, brain and bone surface, the least.
A fala fica entre 500 e 3.000 Hz. A perd: Speech lies between 500 and 3,000 Hz. Noise-induced loss begins just above, which is why it goes unnoticed.
A falta de oxigênio é silenciosa: o cére: A lack of oxygen is silent: the brain feels it before you notice. With vision and oxygen curve simulators.
A fase mais sensível é a **gestação**. D: The most sensitive phase is **pregnancy**. Once the pregnancy is declared, it is recommended that the **fetus receive at most 1 mSv** until the end of pregnancy, and **no more than 0.5 mSv in any one month**. The estimated risk of **fatal cancer** from exposure before birth is **1 in 10,000 per mSv**, higher than that of an adult. In the **first three weeks**, before cells specialize, a particle can kill the embryo, a risk that falls very quickly after the first days. Up to **20 mSv**, no malformations were seen.
A folga deixa o corpo rebater contra o a: Slack lets the body rebound against the seat; a well-adjusted torso harness reduces the rebound and the load on the vertebrae.
A forma de prender o corpo pesa tanto qu: How the body is restrained matters as much as the number. In the British Royal Air Force, the model predicted about **4%** spinal injuries in ejections, and the real rate was **30% to 50%**, because of the **type of harness** and the slack between the body and the seat. A **well-adjusted torso harness** couples the body to the seat and reduces **rebound**, which increases the load on the vertebrae.
A gestante deve informar a gravidez e pa: A pregnant candidate must report the pregnancy and stop flying until the CMA is suspended.
A hiperventilação baixa o gás carbônico: Hyperventilation lowers carbon dioxide and causes tingling and spasms
A hipotermia leva pelo menos meia hora e: Hypothermia takes at least half an hour and, by about 1 hour, leads to unconsciousness. Conserve heat and wait for rescue.
A hipóxia altera o julgamento antes dos: Hypoxia impairs judgment before visible signs appear, and the person may not realize they are in danger.
A hipóxia tira o julgamento antes dos si: Hypoxia takes away judgment before the symptoms
A hipóxia é traiçoeira: **começa sem dor: Hypoxia is treacherous: **it starts without pain and without clear shortness of breath**. Judgment, attention and coordination deteriorate while the person still feels fine. This gap between what one feels and what one can do is the greatest risk on board.
A intensidade se mede em **decibéis (dB): Intensity is measured in **decibels (dB)**, on a **logarithmic** scale: each additional **3 dB** doubles the sound energy, and each **10 dB** multiplies it by ten. To assess the risk to the ear, the **A curve**, **dB(A)**, is used, which weights frequencies the way the ear perceives them. In Brazil, the occupational hazard standard, **NR-15**, requires measuring in dB(A), with slow response, close to the worker's ear.
A investigação mostrou baixa probabilida: Did the workup show a low probability of affecting flight?
A maior parte vem de fora do Sistema Sol: Most of it comes from outside the Solar System: these are **galactic cosmic rays**, probably launched by exploding stars, **supernovae**. They arrive as very fast atomic nuclei: about **85% protons**, **12% alpha particles** (helium nuclei), **2% electrons** and **1% heavier nuclei**. The **Sun** also launches particles, almost only protons, with much lower energy.
A manobra anti-G cansa e pode causar les: The anti-G maneuver is tiring and can cause injury if done at full strength at 1 G
A manobra treinada rendeu cerca de 3 G;: The trained maneuver provided about 3 G; the anti-G suit, about 1 G.
A mesma lógica vale para outras exposiçõ: The same logic applies to other pressure exposures. After training in a **hypobaric chamber**, one also waits **24 hours** before flying. And after an unpressurized flight above 18,000 ft, ideally one should **avoid physical exertion for 24 hours**.
A máscara de colocação rápida dos piloto: The pilots' quick-donning mask: put on with one hand, within 5 seconds.
A máscara dos pilotos pode entregar mais: The pilots' mask can deliver more oxygen than the passengers'; that is why each uses their own. In unpressurized flight, oxygen is **recommended from 10,000 ft by day and above 5,000 ft at night**. The difference comes from the body: **night vision** is among the first functions to worsen with a lack of oxygen (See M2V1 - IV).
A máscara que vaza deixa entrar ar da ca: A leaking mask lets cabin air in and oxygen falls
A norma também avalia o valor da dose de: The standard also assesses the vibration dose value (VDV), which weights jolts.
A névoa da descompressão: a queda brusca: The decompression fog: the sudden drop in pressure and temperature condenses the air's moisture in seconds.
A ordem é fixa: **oxigênio adequado prim: The order is fixed: **adequate oxygen first, system checked and altitude corrected if needed**. Only after ruling out hypoxia is it worth coaching slower breathing. **Breathing into a paper bag is not safe** when this doubt exists.
A partir de 0,5 m/s²: nível de ação. A e: From 0.5 m/s²: action level. The company must take measures to reduce exposure.
A partir de 37,5 °C caem atenção, visão: From 37.5 °C attention, vision and decision-making decline; above 40.6 °C, heatstroke with confusion and coma
A partir de cerca dos 30 anos, a audição: From about age 30, hearing declines between 1,000 and 6,000 Hz and adds to noise-induced loss.
A passagem nasal direita está livre?: Is the right nasal passage clear?
A passagem nasal direita precisa estar l: The right nasal passage must be clear.
A passagem nasal esquerda está livre?: Is the left nasal passage clear?
A passagem nasal esquerda precisa estar: The left nasal passage must be clear.
A perda começa **perto de 4.000 Hz**, ac: The loss begins **near 4,000 Hz**, above the range of conversation, which is why, at first, the person **does not notice**. Only **audiometry** shows the drop. With **age**, hearing also declines, between **1,000 and 6,000 Hz**, from about **age 30**, and the two losses add up. For the US institute of occupational health, **NIOSH**, a worsening of **15 dB** or more at any frequency from 500 to 6,000 Hz, confirmed on a new test within 30 days, is already a **significant threshold shift**.
A porcentagem de oxigênio cai para cerca: The percentage of oxygen falls to about 10%.
A porcentagem de oxigênio continua perto: The percentage of oxygen stays close to 21%, but the pressure falls by half.
A porcentagem de oxigênio no ar diminui: The percentage of oxygen in the air decreases
A pressurização mantém a cabine numa alt: Pressurization keeps the cabin at a lower altitude, but it can fail; supplemental oxygen is the protection for that moment.
A pressurização mantém o corpo numa alti: Pressurization keeps the body at a low cabin altitude (See M1V2 - II). **Decompression** is the loss of this protection: the cabin starts climbing toward the airplane's real altitude. As medições em voo mostram o mesmo quadr: In-flight measurements show the same picture. In a commercial jet, the passenger cabin was between **60 and 65 dB(A)** before takeoff, **80 to 85** in cruise and **75 to 80** on landing. In the cockpits of airline jets and turboprops, the flight average was between **70 and 79 dB(A)**. The sound reaching the pilot's ear through the **headset**, however, can exceed the noise of the cockpit itself (See M1V6 - III). On long flights, this noise weighs on the **comfort** and **well-being** of passengers and crew.

As regras da FAA escalonam o uso. Entre: FAA rules stagger its use. Between **12,500 and 14,000 ft** of cabin altitude, the crew uses oxygen if they stay more than 30 minutes; above **14,000 ft**, the whole time; above **15,000 ft**, **everyone on board** receives oxygen. In pressurized airplanes, above **FL250** there must be at least **10 minutes of oxygen per occupant** for the emergency descent; above **FL350**, one pilot flies wearing a mask, except when two pilots have quick-donning masks, put on with one hand within 5 seconds, up to FL410. The steps follow physiology: the higher the cabin, **the shorter the time of useful consciousness** without oxygen (See M2V1 - III).

Cada ambiente muda a tática. No **desert: Each environment changes the tactics. In the **desert**, the rule is **ration sweat, not water**: stay in the shade, which can be about **22 °C cooler**, work at night and wear **light-colored, loose, layered clothing**. In the **cold**, layers of clothing and insulation from the ground are the shelter (See M1V4 - II). In **water**, breathing control and 1-10-1 apply.

Cada sistema tem um teto. No **fluxo con: Each system has a ceiling. In **continuous flow**, oxygen flows nonstop and mixes with the air, with a reservoir bag on the mask: it is certified up to 41,000 ft, but requires close attention above **25,000 ft**. In **diluter demand**, oxygen flows only on inhalation, mixed or at 100%, and is safe up to **40,000 ft**, as long as the mask seals well: **beards and mustaches get in the way**, and a leaking mask lets cabin air in, and oxygen in the lungs falls without warning. Above that, only **pressure demand** (See M1V2 - IV).
Cada vez que o ser humano voou mais alto: Each time human beings flew higher, faster or farther, the body revealed a new limit.
Cada voo soma uma dose que cresce com o: Each flight adds a dose that grows with **time in the air**, **altitude** and **latitude**. A short, low flight, such as Houston–Austin, half an hour at 20,000 feet, stays below **0.2 µSv**. A long, high flight near the pole, such as **New York–Tokyo**, 13 hours at up to 43,000 feet, exceeds **55 µSv**.

The FAA's **CARI** programs, with **CARI-7** as the recommended version, calculate a flight's dose from the route, altitude and date. Solar events, however, are not forecast in advance: the FAA's medical institute issues **solar radiation alerts** using data from the US space weather agency (**NOAA**). During an alert, **descending** at high latitudes greatly reduces the dose, especially if the response is quick. For the body, the rule is always the same: **less time, less altitude and less latitude add up to less dose**.

In **Brazil**, since 2024 the basic radiological protection standard of **CNEN**, **NN 3.01**, recognizes the exposure of aircrew: for those flying above **28,000 feet**, the company must **estimate the annual dose** of each crew member from routes and flight hours, **keep and provide the records**, **inform the risks** and advise **pregnant crew members** to declare the pregnancy immediately, with a **reference level of 5 mSv per year**.

As a result, daily exposure would exceed **85 dB(A)** on **30% to 40% of duty days**. All the risk came from the **open headset**, which does not seal the ear; on short flights, the authors predicted no risk. In other words, the pilot's ear can suffer more from the headset than from the cockpit.

No Brasil, o limite legal está no **Anex: In Brazil, the legal limit is in **Annex 1 of NR-15**: **85 dB(A) for 8 hours** a day. O **altímetro** é um barômetro: mede a p: The **altimeter** is a barometer: it measures pressure and converts it into altitude using this yardstick. Set to **1,013.25 hPa**, it shows **pressure altitude**, the reference for flight levels and operational calculations. O **assento ejetável** tira o piloto de: The **ejection seat** gets the pilot out of an airplane that is out of control. An **explosive charge** fires the seat up the rails, a **rocket** carries it away from the airplane and the **parachute** opens on its own: in the **Brazilian Air Force Gripen**, all in about **1.8 seconds**. The seats of a single manufacturer have already saved **more than 7,700 crew members**; the model used in the **Gripen**, the **Super Tucano** and the **AMX**, more than **1,400**.
O **tempo de consciência útil (TCU)** é: The **time of useful consciousness (TUC)** is the time a person still has, after oxygen drops, to recognize the problem and act correctly. **It is not the time until fainting**: judgment and coordination fail first.
O **tempo em altitude** é o fator de ris: **Time at altitude** is the strongest risk factor. Added to it are a **rapid climb**, **repeated exposures** above 18,000 ft within a few hours, **physical exertion** at altitude, a **recent joint injury**, **intense cold**, **body fat** (which stores more nitrogen), **age**, the effects of **alcohol** and a **recent dive** (See M1V3 - III).
O **traje anti-G** infla bolsas nas pern: The **anti-G suit** inflates bladders on the legs and abdomen, squeezes the veins and holds blood in the trunk: it provides about **1 G**. O **−Gz** faz o caminho inverso: o sangu: **−Gz** works the other way: blood pools in the head, vision turns **red** and unconsciousness can come quickly. Tolerance is also lowered by **dehydration, fatigue, hunger, medications, a sedentary lifestyle and smoking**. In G-LOC accidents, **little experience in the airplane, being under 30 and a poorly performed anti-G maneuver** accounted for 72% of cases.
O +Gz empurra o sangue para as pernas e: +Gz pushes blood toward the legs and takes it away from the brain and eyes.

Over **South America and the Caribbean**, between 29,000 and 41,000 feet, the calculated average rate is between **2.65 and 2.95 µSv per hour**, depending on the solar cycle, below the roughly 4.0 of London–New York. In a typical year of flights in the region, the dose adds up to **1.45 to 1.67 mSv**. On domestic flights, **Rio–São Paulo** adds about **1.8 µSv**, and the longest legs reach **8.8 µSv**; those who fly only within the country average close to **0.76 mSv per year**.

Before the complete blackout there is **A-LOC**, almost loss of consciousness, with the pilot confused and slow, but awake.

O calor age em degraus. Com a temperatur: Heat acts in steps. With a core temperature between **37.5 and 37.8 °C**, **heat stress** comes: coordination, attention, vision, decision-making and caution decline, precisely what flight demands. Between **38.3 and 40.6 °C**, **heat exhaustion** brings fatigue, nausea, dizziness, cramps, rapid breathing and even fainting. **Above 40.6 °C**, temperature control fails: this is **heatstroke**, with confusion, strange behavior and coma. Sweating stops, and the skin becomes **hot and dry**.
O calor anda junto com a **desidratação*: Heat goes hand in hand with **dehydration**. About **two thirds of the body is water**. **Thirst only appears once about 2% of body weight has been lost**; at around 5%, fatigue, nausea and emotional instability arrive. With further loss, headache, confusion, delirium and kidney failure appear.

The protection is the **right, well-fitted** helmet, secured by the chin strap, and a **strengthened neck**. In passenger airplanes, the role of the helmet falls to the **seat**: where the head can strike, the HIC may not exceed 1,000.

O ruído forte lesa as **células ciliadas: Loud noise injures the **hair cells** of the cochlea. First comes **temporary loss**: after a few hours above **90 dB** without protection, hearing drops and usually returns within a few hours. With repetition, the injury becomes **permanent**: exposures above 90 dB, **8 hours or more a day, for several years**, lead to a **sensorineural** loss that **cannot be reversed**. This is **noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL)**.

The human ear picks up about **20 to 20,000 hertz (Hz)**, vibrations per second, and is most sensitive between **500 and 4,000 Hz**; **conversation** lies between **500 and 3,000 Hz**.

Os estudos com tripulantes ainda não sep: Studies of crew members still cannot separate radiation from the profession's other factors. O *: Other criteria are stricter. **NIOSH** recommends the same **85 dB(A) over 8 hours**, but the time is halved every **3 dB**, the **equal energy** rule, and allows no exposure above **140 dB(A)**. By NIOSH estimates, 40 years of work at 85 dB(A) leave **8%** of workers with significant hearing loss; at **90 dB(A)**, **25%**. This is the limit of **OSHA**, the US occupational safety agency, which uses the 5 dB rule and requires a hearing conservation program from 85 dB(A). Três fatores mudam a dose. A **altitude*: Three factors change the dose. **Altitude**: the higher, the greater the rate. **Latitude**: the Earth's magnetic field deflects particles, with maximum protection at the **geomagnetic equator** and none near the **poles**, where radiation reaches about **double**; at 35,000 feet, over Alaska, it is double that of Miami and triple that of Guam, in the Pacific. And the **solar cycle**, of about **11 years**: with a more active Sun, fewer galactic rays reach the Earth.

Na **apneia obstrutiva do sono**, a garg: In **obstructive sleep apnea**, the throat closes several times during sleep, breathing stops and blood oxygen drops with each pause. Sleep becomes fragmented, and the next day brings **sleepiness**, inattention and errors. Weight matters a lot: according to the FAA, more than **90%** of people with a **BMI of 40 or more** have apnea requiring treatment, but up to **30%** of people with apnea have a **BMI below 30**. A receding chin, a large tongue or tonsils, **hard-to-control blood pressure** on more than two medications, **diabetes** and **atrial fibrillation** also raise the risk.
Na **asma**, os brônquios inflamam e se: In **asthma**, the airways become inflamed and close in attacks that come and go. In **COPD**, which includes **chronic bronchitis** and **emphysema**, airflow is permanently limited and the lung loses reserve. The cabin is pressurized to at most **8,000 ft (2,438 m)**, an altitude at which a healthy person keeps saturation **above 90%**. Someone who leaves the ground with low saturation starts the flight closer to the part of the curve where **each drop in pressure lowers saturation more** (See M2V1 - I).
Na DPOC, o alerta vem dos números do sol: In COPD, the warning comes from the ground numbers. A **resting saturation of 95% or less**, shortness of breath with everyday efforts (**MRC scale 3 or more**) or a drop **below 84%** on a walk test indicate that the person may need **in-flight oxygen** and should take the altitude simulation test (See M2V1 - IX). In emphysema, air trapped in **bullae** expands about **38%** at 8,000 ft (See M1V1 - II). In asthma, the risk is an **attack far from medical care**, with no way to land right away.

O **passageiro** com apneia pode voar, d: A **passenger** with apnea can fly as long as they bring their treatment: the **CPAP** goes in hand luggage, with a letter from the physician and **prior airline approval** for the device and batteries. For **crew members**, the FAA considers apnea **disqualifying** until **effective treatment** is shown; those under treatment receive a special issuance with follow-up, and those the examiner classifies as **high risk** have **90 days** to send the sleep evaluation. Symptoms that threaten safety right away make the examiner **defer** the certificate. RBAC 67 has no specific item for apnea; it falls under the rule for conditions affecting flight safety, at the examiner's discretion.
O **teste de simulação de altitude**, ou: The **altitude simulation test**, or hypoxic challenge test, shows on the ground how the body will react in the cabin. Below that, it is **recommended**, adjusted to keep saturation at least at **85%** in adults. Para o **passageiro**, a British Thoraci: For the **passenger**, the British Thoracic Society is clear: **do not fly until 7 days after full resolution on X-ray**. An untreated closed pneumothorax generally precludes flying. After **thoracotomy with surgical pleurodesis**, recurrence is so low that no extra restriction applies; with **video-assisted thoracoscopy**, the reported recurrence is about **4 times higher**. After **thoracic surgery**, the wait is **4 weeks** after drain removal for non-essential trips, or **2 weeks** if the trip is essential. After a **lung biopsy**, a pleural procedure or a **bronchoscopy with biopsy**, **1 week**, counted from resolution if there was a pneumothorax.
Para o **passageiro**, a regra é a estab: For the **passenger**, the rule is stability: fly only with the disease **stable** and reliever inhaler use **at the usual level**. After a **COPD worsening**, the British Thoracic Society considers it prudent to wait **6 weeks**, although data are scarce. For **crew members**, the rules are stricter. In RBAC 67, **asthma** is among the conditions that make the applicant **unfit** for 1st class, and so is **chronic lung disease**, unless an investigation shows a low chance of affecting the flight. The FAA issues the certificate for **controlled** asthma: symptoms on up to **2 days a week**, at most **2 visits** for attacks and **2 courses of oral corticosteroids** a year, **no hospital admission** in the past year and **FEV1 and FVC of 80% or more** of predicted before the bronchodilator. In COPD, the decision always belongs to the FAA.
Para o **tripulante**, o prazo é mais lo: For **crew members**, the wait is longer. In RBAC 67, an **unresolved pneumothorax** makes the applicant **unfit**, and bullous lung disease is at the examiner's discretion. Under the FAA, a **spontaneous** pneumothorax requires an X-ray showing resolution and confirmation that there are **no blebs** at risk of a new episode, and the decision belongs to the FAA itself; those with **more than one episode** return only after the surgery that corrects the cause, usually **3 months** after it. For a **traumatic** pneumothorax, the FAA issues the certificate **3 months after resolution**. New Zealand's authority considers an episode significant, without surgery, if it occurred less than **5 years** ago for Class 1 and less than **3 years** ago for Class 2.

No **mal agudo da montanha**, a dor de c: In **acute mountain sickness**, headache comes with at least one of these signs: loss of appetite, dizziness, fatigue, nausea or vomiting. It starts within **2 to 12 hours**, often on the first night, and resolves in **1 to 3 days** without further ascent. **High-altitude cerebral edema** is the severe form, with confusion, loss of balance and drowsiness, and can lead to coma within **24 hours**. **High-altitude pulmonary edema** begins with cough, exaggerated shortness of breath on exertion and reduced performance; untreated, it worsens over **1 to 2 days**, and saturations of **50% to 70%** are common.

O mal da altitude aparece quando a subid: Altitude illness appears when the ascent is faster than adaptation. Any unacclimatized person who will **sleep at 2,450 m or higher** is at risk. In Colorado, about **25%** of visitors who sleep above that altitude develop **acute mountain sickness**; with a rapid arrival by plane above **3,400 m**, the rate approaches **50%**.

For those who fly, the rule applies at the destination. The passenger who lands in a high city and the **crew member** who stays overnight there arrive unacclimatized, because the cabin does not prepare the body to sleep at altitude. A crew member with symptoms does not take the next flight: operating with a condition that prevents safe operation is prohibited by the FAA, and ANAC forbids exercising the license with decreased fitness.

**Arritmia** é o coração fora do ritmo:: **Arrhythmia** is the heart out of rhythm: fast, slow or irregular. The most common in adults is **atrial fibrillation**, in which the atria quiver instead of contracting. It may be **paroxysmal**, with episodes that stop on their own in under 24 hours, **persistent**, lasting more than 7 days and only returning to normal with treatment, or **permanent**, when normal rhythm no longer returns. In **atrial flutter**, the atrium beats close to **300 times a minute**, and the ventricle often at **150**.

Na **doença coronariana**, placas de gor: In **coronary disease**, fatty plaques narrow the **coronary arteries**, the arteries that feed the heart itself. **Angina** is chest pain when the muscle asks for more blood than the artery delivers; a **heart attack** is the death of part of the muscle when the artery closes. Treatment opens the artery from inside, with a **stent** during **angioplasty**, or creates a detour with **bypass surgery**. In the cabin, blood arrives with less oxygen (See M2V2 - I), and anyone with a narrow artery has less margin.
Na **insuficiência cardíaca**, o coração: In **heart failure**, the heart does not pump the blood the body needs, and fluid builds up in the lungs and legs. Severity is measured by the **NYHA functional class**: in **I**, there is no limitation; in **II**, mild symptoms with ordinary activities; in **III**, symptoms with less than ordinary activities; in **IV**, symptoms even at rest. In the cabin, with less oxygen in the air (See M2V2 - I), those already at the limit feel **short of breath** sooner.
Na **trombose venosa profunda**, um coág: In **deep vein thrombosis**, a clot forms in a deep vein, almost always in the **leg**. If it breaks loose and reaches the lung, it becomes a **pulmonary embolism**, which can kill. Hours **seated**, with legs bent and little movement, leave blood pooled in the calf veins (See M2V2 - I).

O risco do voo existe, mas é pequeno: no: The risk from flying exists, but it is small: on flights of **more than 4 hours**, one study found **1 case in 4,656** journeys, and another, **1 in 6,000**. A **direção** muda tudo. Voando para o *: **Direction** changes everything. Flying **east**, the wall clock jumps forward and the body has to **advance** its own: sleep and wake earlier. Flying **west**, the body has to **delay** its clock: sleep and wake later. Because the internal clock has a natural cycle **slightly longer than 24 hours**, **delaying is easier than advancing**.
A **luz** é o tratamento mais forte. A l: **Light** is the strongest treatment. Bright light **after the lowest point of the clock**, about 2 to 4 hours before your usual wake time, **advances** the clock; light **in the evening** **delays** it. Going **east**, seek **morning light** and avoid evening light, with sunglasses and closed curtains. Going **west**, avoid bright light early in the morning and make use of late-day light. At the destination, go out and get **daylight on local time**.
A **melatonina** ajuda quando tomada na: **Melatonin** helps when taken at the **right time**. Doses of **0.5 to 1 mg** are usually enough; more than **5 mg** is not recommended, because the excess keeps acting at the wrong time. Taken about **90 minutes before bedtime** on destination time, it **advances** the clock and helps those who flew **east**; taken in the morning, it **delays** it and helps those who flew **west**. Between midnight and 5 a.m. on the internal clock it **has no effect**, and at the wrong time it **worsens** the mismatch. Outside pharmacies, the real dose may not match the label.

The FRMS has **four components**: policy and documentation, risk management, safety assurance, and promotion, with training and communication.

A fadiga depende de três coisas: há **qu: Fatigue depends on three things: **how long** the person has been awake, **how long** they have been working and **what time** the body clock shows. Performance is stable for the first **16 hours** awake; after that reactions slow, and between **18 and 20 hours** the decline is clear. Pilots departing at night after **13.5 hours** awake reacted more slowly than those departing in the morning, with **3.5 hours** awake.

After **2 nights of 4 hours**, **leptin**, which brings satiety, fell about **18%**, **ghrelin**, which brings hunger, rose about **28%**, hunger increased **24%** and the craving for carbohydrates **32%**. After **5 nights of 4 hours**, glucose tolerance fell about **43%** and insulin sensitivity **24%**.

Two drivers decide when we feel sleepy. The first is **sleep pressure**, which builds with every hour awake and only falls with sleep. The second is the **biological clock**, run by the **suprachiasmatic nucleus**, a group of neurons in the brain that receives **light** through the eyes and sets the rhythm of almost every organ. Without cues from the environment, the clock runs on **24 to 28 hours**; light keeps it set to the day.

The night is made of **cycles of about 90 minutes** that alternate **non-REM sleep**, lighter in stages 1 and 2 and **deep** in stage 3, and **REM sleep**, the dreaming sleep. In young adults, about **55%** of the night is light sleep, **20%** deep sleep and **25%** REM. Deep sleep dominates the start of the night; REM grows toward dawn. Most adults need **7 to 9 hours**, and the FAA uses **8 hours** as the reference.

Na prática, o corpo se ajusta em média *: In practice, the body adjusts on average **1.5 hours a day** after flying **west** and only **1 hour a day** after flying **east**. Six time zones east may take close to a week; six west, about four days. Moreover, each organ adjusts at a different pace: for a few days, sleep, temperature, hormones and digestion are **out of sync with one another**.

No Brasil, a **Lei do Aeronauta** fixa o: In Brazil, the **Aeronaut Law** sets the limits for scheduled air transport. Per duty period, it allows **8 flight hours** for a single crew, **11** for an augmented crew and **14** for a relief crew, with duty periods of **9, 12 and 16 hours**. On jets, the limit is **80 flight hours a month** and **800 a year**. At most **2 consecutive night duties** and **4 in 168 hours** are allowed, counting night as **midnight to 6 a.m.** on home-base time. The law also lets the authority change the limits through **fatigue risk management**.

O **cortisol**, o hormônio do despertar: **Cortisol**, the hormone of waking and stress, does the opposite: it **peaks in the early morning**, falls through the day, is **low in the late afternoon and early night** and rises sharply **in the late small hours**, preparing for waking. This rhythm is driven mainly by the clock, not by sleep: someone who stays awake all night still has cortisol rising in the morning.
O **jet lag** é o descompasso entre o **: **Jet lag** is the mismatch between the **biological clock** and **local time** after crossing time zones quickly. It counts from **2 time zones** and brings, within **1 to 2 days**, **insomnia** or **daytime sleepiness**, tiredness, difficulty concentrating, malaise and **stomach and bowel** problems. In one survey, **68%** of business travelers often had these symptoms.
O **repouso** cresce com a jornada: **12: **Rest** grows with the duty period: **12 hours** after up to 12 hours of duty, **16 hours** after 12 to 15 hours and **24 hours** after more than 15. Anyone crossing **3 or more time zones** in one direction gets **2 extra hours per time zone**, at home base, and the month must have at least **10 days off**. In the US, the FAA requires **10 hours** of rest with **8 consecutive hours of sleep opportunity**, **30 hours free** every week and, after crossing more than **60° of longitude** and spending more than a week away, **56 hours** with **3 nights** of sleep.
O **álcool** engana: faz adormecer mais: **Alcohol** is deceptive: it makes you fall asleep faster, but **2 drinks** delay REM and **3 or more** make you wake early. **Caffeine** takes **15 to 30 minutes** to act and lasts up to **5 hours**; daily users lose part of the effect. The **nap** is the strongest countermeasure: **10 minutes** already improve alertness, but naps longer than **45 minutes** bring **sleep inertia**, a sluggishness of **20 minutes or more** on waking; allow at least **10 to 15 minutes** before a safety task.

O relógio biológico é também um **relógi: The biological clock is also a **hormonal clock**. **Melatonin**, produced by the **pineal gland** in the dark, rises about **2 hours before bedtime**, stays high for about **12 hours** and **peaks around 3 to 4 a.m.** Daylight suppresses it; that is why **light** is the clock's main synchronizer, and melatonin signals to the body that it is night.
O relógio cria horários fortes. A **jane: The clock creates strong time slots. The **window of circadian low**, between about **2 and 6 a.m.**, coincides with the body's **lowest temperature** and is the worst time to work: errors rise sharply **between 2 and 4 a.m.** There is a second dip **in the afternoon, around 3 to 5 p.m.** In the hours before bedtime, by contrast, the clock holds wakefulness, and going to bed early yields little sleep.

O resultado tem nome: **fadiga**. Para a: The result has a name: **fatigue**. For ICAO, it is physical or mental capability reduced by **sleep loss**, **extended wakefulness**, **circadian phase** or **workload**, to the point of impairing alertness and safe operation. It can be **transient**, resolved by one good sleep, or **cumulative**, when recovery is incomplete day after day.

Remédios para dormir, como o **zolpidem*: Sleeping pills such as **zolpidem** and **eszopiclone** can help the passenger for a few nights, with medical guidance. **Antihistamines** and **long-acting sedatives** impair alertness and balance and should be avoided, including on board. **Crew members** follow their own rules: on short layovers they **stay on home time**; ICAO **does not recommend** melatonin for crew in general; and the Aeronaut Law gives **2 extra hours of rest per time zone** when the trip crosses **3 or more time zones** in one direction.

**Esticar o dia ou dormir?** Ficar acord: **Stretch the day or sleep?** Staying awake during the **local day** builds sleep pressure and helps you sleep on the destination's night. Going **west**, hold off sleep until **local bedtime**. If daytime sleep is unavoidable, limit it to **2 or 3 hours**; just to restore alertness, **20 to 30 minutes** is enough. In the **first 2 days**, sleep comes most easily in the **early afternoon of home time**, the post-lunch dip that travels with you. Before a whole night of flying or work, **sleep during the day**. On board, you sleep better with **less alcohol and caffeine** and an **eye mask and earplugs**.
**Outras dicas.** O **exercício** aument: **Other tips.** **Exercise** increases alertness: preferably outdoors and in daylight, adding the light, but no vigorous effort in the **2 hours before sleep**. Drink **water** on the flight and at the destination: dehydration worsens the symptoms, and **alcohol** and **caffeine** dehydrate; alcohol also makes you fall asleep faster but **fragments** sleep. Take your **bedtime routine** with you. Everyone reacts differently: try the strategies, keep the ones that work for you and remember that **anxiety** and **worries** worsen sleep away from home. Official sources do not recommend a special anti-jet-lag diet; what counts is **when** you eat.

A **luz** é o tratamento mais forte. A l: **Light** is the strongest treatment. Bright light **after the lowest point of the clock**, about 2 to 4 hours before your usual wake time, **advances** the clock; light **in the evening** **delays** it. Going **east**, seek **morning light** and avoid evening light, with sunglasses and closed curtains. Going **west**, avoid bright light early in the morning and make use of late-day light. At the destination, go out and get **daylight on local time**. The ideal timing of light also depends on the **number of time zones**: when there are many, the destination morning may fall before the lowest point of the body clock, and it is worth using a jet lag calculator or seeking advice.
A **melatonina** ajuda quando tomada na: **Melatonin** helps when taken at the **right time**. Doses of **0.5 to 1 mg** are usually enough; more than **5 mg** is not recommended, because the excess keeps acting at the wrong time. Taken about **90 minutes before bedtime** on destination time, it **advances** the clock and helps those who flew **east**; taken when the body clock reads **morning**, it **delays** it and helps those who flew **west**. When the body's own melatonin is already high, during the internal clock's night, it **has no effect**, and at the wrong time it **worsens** the mismatch. Outside pharmacies, the real dose may not match the label.
A hora exata da luz e da melatonina depe: The exact timing of light and melatonin depends on the number of time zones. On trips across many time zones, use a jet lag calculator or seek medical advice.

**Como aproveitar o repouso.** No pernoi: **Making the most of rest.** On a layover, the priority is the **opportunity to sleep**: a dark, quiet, cool room, a reliable alarm and sleep set for the hours when the clock helps. In the US, a crew member who cannot get **8 consecutive hours** of sleep opportunity must **notify the operator**. On board, lie down even if you are not sleepy: the bunk rarely yields more than **5 hours** of sleep, and two periods of **3 to 5 hours** work better than one of 8. On waking from the bunk or from controlled rest, allow **10 to 15 minutes** for inertia to pass before taking over. After runs of night duties or long duty periods, recovery takes **2 consecutive nights** of unrestricted sleep.
**Como prevenir e amenizar a fadiga.** O: **How to prevent and ease fatigue.** Sleep is the only cure, and it starts **before the duty period**: before working all night, **sleep during the day**. A **nap of 25 to 30 minutes** before leaving helps; even **10 minutes** already improve alertness. On duty, **caffeine** acts within **15 to 30 minutes** and lasts up to **5 hours**; use it when you need it, not out of habit. **5-minute breaks**, getting up and talking break the monotony, and **controlled rest** on the flight deck is only valid where the authority and the operator allow it. In the small hours, between **2 and 4 a.m.**, double your checks. After the duty period, recover: it takes at least **2 nights** of unrestricted sleep.
**Como proteger os hormônios.** A **luz*: **How to protect your hormones.** **Light** controls melatonin: bright light in the morning and little bright light in the hours before bed. **Growth hormone** depends on the deep sleep of the **early night**, so the first hours of sleep are worth the most. The hunger that appears after short nights is partly **high ghrelin and low leptin**: knowing this helps you not to mistake sleepiness for hunger. Because glucose tolerance is lower **in the small hours**, night workers do better with light meals at those hours and the main meal in the daytime. No supplement replaces sleep: after a few short nights, metabolism already changes.
**Como usar o relógio a seu favor.** A n: **Using the clock to your advantage.** Sleep need varies from person to person, but nobody can train themselves to need less: losing a few hours a night already impairs performance after **2 or 3 days**. With **age**, sleep quality worsens, and the same hours yield lighter sleep. The clock's day has strong and weak hours: performance is worst between **1 and 5 a.m.**, the second dip comes in the **mid-afternoon**, and in the hours before bedtime the clock holds wakefulness. Plan sleep, work and demanding tasks with this map in mind.
**O que aumenta a fadiga.** Além do sono: **What increases fatigue.** Besides sleep and the time of day, **age**, **health**, the **type of task** (monotonous or demanding, physical or mental), **time on task**, **workload**, the **environment** (heat, cold, noise) and **medicines** all count. On the flight deck, the **number and composition of the crew**, **acclimatization to the time zone**, the **previous duty**, the **opportunity to rest** before and during the flight and **recovery** afterwards also count. An often forgotten factor: arriving for duty **already short of sleep**.
A única cura para a fadiga é **dormir**,: The only cure for fatigue is **sleep**, and sleep starts before going to bed. Sleep when the clock helps: protect the **small hours** of the body clock, when sleep comes most easily, and prefer to nap in the body clock's **mid-afternoon**, around **3 to 5 p.m.** Block **light** with curtains or a mask, use **earplugs** or white noise, keep the room near **21 °C**, avoid **vigorous exercise** in the 2 hours before and a **heavy meal** 1 to 2 hours before, and follow a bedtime **routine** away from home too. Use a **reliable alarm**, so you do not sleep afraid of oversleeping, and allow time to **wind down** after stressful tasks. Keep caffeine, **tobacco** and food away from the hours before bed.

**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes de v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before traveling, check that the heart failure is **compensated**: no shortness of breath at rest, no new swelling and no rapid weight gain. In class **III or IV**, arrange **oxygen** with the airline through the MEDIF. Carry your medicines in **hand luggage**; anyone on a **diuretic** chooses a seat near the toilet instead of skipping the dose. Avoid exertion and heavy bags at the airport, and move your legs on a long flight. Shortness of breath that worsens on board calls for telling the crew immediately.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Mantenha o: **How to prevent and ease it.** Keep your **echocardiogram** up to date and know your valve type: a **mechanical** one requires lifelong anticoagulation, and the dose must stay on schedule while traveling too (See M2V8 - IV). Anyone with **cyanotic** heart disease or **pulmonary hypertension** arranges **oxygen** with the airline before boarding. Avoid exertion at the airport and ask for help with bags. New shortness of breath, fainting or chest pain are warning signs, on the ground and on board.

**How to prevent and ease it.** Keep rhythm medicines and the **anticoagulant** on the right schedule, adjusting them to the time zones with your doctor (See M2V8 - IV); a delayed dose can leave the heart or the blood unprotected. Anyone with a **pacemaker** or **defibrillator** can fly when stable: interference with aircraft systems or with security screening is **very unlikely** with common devices. New palpitations on board, dizziness or fainting call for telling the crew immediately. For crew, the work-up includes the **Holter**, the **echocardiogram** and the **thyroid**, and return follows the waiting time of each procedure.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Meça a pre: **How to prevent and ease it.** Measure your blood pressure on **different days**, always at rest, and take the readings to your appointment. Do not stop or change your medicine on your own before the trip; carry the tablets in **hand luggage** and keep the interval between doses when crossing time zones (See M2V8 - IV). In the first days of a new medicine, **stand up slowly** from your seat, because the drop in pressure on standing can cause dizziness. Crew return to flying only when control is **stable and free of side effects**, and check that the medicine is accepted by the authority: **centrally acting** ones are accepted by neither the FAA nor ICAO.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Respeite o: **How to prevent and ease it.** Respect the **waiting time** after the event: it changes with the type of treatment and whether there were complications. Carry your medicines in **hand luggage** and **do not stop the antiplatelet** on your own, not even to travel. If angina appears with light exertion, arrange **oxygen** with the airline. Avoid carrying heavy bags and rushing at the airport: ask for help and arrive with time to spare. **Quitting smoking**, the **statin** and blood pressure control reduce the risk of a new event. Chest pain on board calls for telling the crew immediately.
**Como se preparar para voar com o coraç: **Getting ready to fly with a heart condition.** Carry your **medicines in hand luggage**, with the prescription and dose list, and adjust the times when crossing time zones (See M2V8 - IV). If your doctor prescribes **oxygen on board**, arrange it with the airline before the flight, through the **MEDIF**. On a long flight, **walk** and move your legs (See M2V2 - VII). **Chest pain, shortness of breath, palpitations or fainting** on board call for telling the crew immediately. For crew, the **electrocardiogram** follows age and class, and any worsening of health must be reported to the examiner before the next flight.

**Quem precisa de mais cuidado.** O risc: **Who needs more care.** High risk does not come from the flight alone but from its combination with other factors: **previous thrombosis**, recent **surgery**, hospitalization or trauma, **active cancer**, **pregnancy** and the postpartum period, estrogen-containing **hormones**, **obesity**, thrombophilia and reduced mobility. The **longer** the flight, the more each one counts. People with these factors plan ahead: a **compression stocking** and a talk with their doctor about **heparin**. Anyone already on an **anticoagulant** keeps the doses on schedule, including when crossing time zones (See M2V8 - IV), and needs nothing more for the flight beyond the measures for everyone.
**Como ganhar tempo.** O TCU depende da: **How to gain time.** TUC depends on the source and the person: for ICAO, it is close to **10 minutes at 20,000 ft**, **2.5 minutes or less at 25,000 ft** and about **30 seconds at 30,000 ft**; that is why the numbers are a warning, not a deadline. Time is gained before the problem: knowing the flight altitude and its TUC, knowing where the mask is and practicing the move. **Altitude chamber** training shows your own TUC safely. For crew in unpressurized aircraft, the US rule requires oxygen after **30 minutes between 12,500 and 14,000 ft**, all the time **above 14,000 ft**, and for all occupants **above 15,000 ft**.
**Como prevenir cada tipo.** A **hipóxic: **How to prevent each type.** **Hypoxic** hypoxia is prevented with pressurization and oxygen at the right altitudes. **Hypemic** hypoxia, by treating anemia before flying (See M2V11) and suspecting **carbon monoxide** in piston aircraft: headache, dizziness or drowsiness with the heater on call for oxygen and landing. The **stagnant** hypoxia of accelerations is prevented with the anti-G straining maneuver and suit (See M1V7). **Histotoxic** hypoxia appears mainly in fire smoke, where **cyanide** and carbon monoxide add up: respiratory protection and a quick exit (See M3V8).
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** O treiname: **How to prevent and ease it.** Chamber training teaches you to tell hypoxia from hyperventilation and shows how your own body responds. In stressful situations, such as severe turbulence or an emergency, notice fast breathing early. Faced with symptoms at altitude, the sequence does not change: **oxygen first**, system and pressurization checked, altitude corrected. Once hypoxia is excluded, **slow your breathing** deliberately until the symptoms pass. Never use a **paper bag** in flight, because it can worsen an unrecognized hypoxia.
**Como proteger o caminho do oxigênio.**: **How to protect the path of oxygen.** Each stage has its own protection. In the **air**, pressurization or supplemental oxygen; the FAA recommends oxygen above **10,000 ft by day** and above **5,000 ft at night**, and ICAO notes that above **10,000 ft** cabin altitude crew must use oxygen. In the **alveolus**, control lung disease before flying (See M2V1 - VI). In the **blood**, treat **anemia** and avoid **carbon monoxide** (See M2V1 - II). In the **tissue**, look after the circulation. Saturation falls with altitude in a predictable way: about **93%** at 8,000 ft, **89%** at 10,000 ft and **80%** at 15,000 ft in people without disease.
**Como reconhecer e agir.** Aprenda a su: **How to recognize it and act.** Learn your **hypoxia signature** in chamber training: it tends to repeat and is the fastest alarm. At night, vision is the first to suffer, and the FAA recommends oxygen from **above 5,000 ft**. At altitude, any strange symptom, such as headache, dizziness, warmth in the face, dimmed vision or yawning, calls for **oxygen first** and only then investigation. On the flight deck, agree with your colleague to watch each other: bluish lips may be absent, but **confusion** and **slowness** show.

**Como equalizar.** Na subida, em geral: **How to equalize.** On the climb, there is usually nothing to do. On the descent, start **early** and repeat: swallow, yawn, chew or tense your throat; if that is not enough, close your mouth, pinch your nose and blow gently against the closed nostrils, the **Valsalva maneuver**. Do not sleep during the descent. Babies suffer more: **breastfeeding** on the climb and descent protects the child from pain. If the ear blocks, keep trying before the outside pressure rises further.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Antes do v: **How to prevent and ease it.** Before the flight, check your nose: blocked or with a cold, crew **do not fly** and passengers consider postponing. Start equalizing **early** on the descent and do not sleep through it. If the ear blocks and hurts, tell the crew and keep doing the maneuvers. After the flight, pain that does not go away, **fluid discharge**, **hearing loss** or **vertigo** call for medical assessment. Anyone using **insert ear protectors** checks the ventilation channel: a tight insert favors barotrauma.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Respeite o: **How to prevent and ease it.** Respect the surgeon's waiting time and, for crew, the authority's. After ear surgery, treat any cold before flying and equalize more carefully on the descent. Anyone with repeated or severe vertigo in flight is referred to an **ENT specialist** with aviation experience. **Passengers** who had ear surgery confirm with the surgeon when they can fly.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Termine o: **How to prevent and ease it.** Finish dental treatment **before** being exposed to pressure changes, and schedule procedures away from trips. Crew have a **dental check every 6 months**. Anyone having treatment over several visits asks for a **well-sealed temporary filling**. After a sinus lift, prefer to return by land or sea; if flying is unavoidable, wait at least 2 weeks and confirm the sinus has no symptoms. Carry the **painkiller** recommended by the dentist if the flight cannot wait.
**Como prevenir e amenizar.** Trate a **: **How to prevent and ease it.** Treat your **allergy** with your usual medicine and look after your nose before the trip. Do not fly with a cold. On the descent, keep up the ear maneuvers, which also help the nose. Anyone with **recurrent sinusitis**, polyps or concha bullosa talks to the ENT specialist: treatment often solves the problem in flight. Pain in the upper teeth that only appears in flight may come from the sinus, not the tooth.
**Como proteger a audição.** Use **prote: **How to protect your hearing.** Use **ear protection** whenever noise is loud (See M1V6 - III). **Earmuffs** reduce about **35 dB** on average; **insert** protectors must fit well and have a clear ventilation channel; the two together reach about **55 dB**, the maximum before sound reaches the ear through the skull bones. Headsets with **active noise reduction** work only on low frequencies, up to **1,200 Hz**, and need passive protection too. Keep the headset volume as low as still lets you understand, keep protectors clean and do not use them with an inflamed ear. Before audiometry, spend some time **away from noise**.
**Não voe hoje** com dor de dente que pi: **Do not fly today** with a toothache that worsens with pressure, a temporary filling or before the waiting time for the procedure. The dentist examines the tooth, tests **pulp vitality** and orders an **X-ray** to find decay, a failed filling or a root lesion.
**Não voe hoje** com resfriado, nariz en: **Do not fly today** with a cold, blocked nose, earache, a full ear that will not clear or vertigo. The doctor looks at the **eardrum** and grades it on the Teed scale, tests the **Valsalva maneuver**, orders **audiometry** if there is hearing loss and examines balance if there is vertigo.
**Não voe hoje** com sinusite, nariz ent: **Do not fly today** with sinusitis, a blocked nose or facial pain. The doctor examines the nose, palpates the sinuses, asks about **sprays** and **antihistamines** in use and, if needed, orders an **X-ray** or **CT scan**.
**Não voe hoje** com vertigem, perfuraçã: **Do not fly today** with vertigo, a recent perforation or ear surgery without clearance. The doctor examines the eardrum with a **pneumatic otoscope**, tests the **Valsalva**, orders **audiometry** and, if there is vertigo, **balance tests**.
**Não voe** como tripulante sem o audiog: **Do not fly** as crew without an up-to-date audiogram or with a new, unassessed hearing loss. The doctor orders **pure-tone audiometry** of each ear, the **voice** test in a quiet room and, if needed, the **speech-in-noise** test.
**Remédios.** O passageiro pode usar **d: **Medicines.** Passengers may use an **oral or nasal decongestant** to relieve symptoms and keep taking their usual **allergy medicine**. A **barodontalgia** é a dor de dente pro: **Barodontalgia** is toothache caused by pressure change. It is not a disease in itself: it appears in a tooth that **already had a problem**, such as **decay**, a **failed filling**, **pulp inflammation**, a **dead pulp** or a **root lesion**. About **one third** of cases come from a **recent filling**. Among crews on military transport flights, **7%** reported at least one episode.
A **vertigem** verdadeira é a sensação d: True **vertigo** is the sensation of spinning. In flight, **alternobaric vertigo** appears on descent when one ear equalizes before the other; a **perilymph fistula** is pressure injury to the inner ear. Outside flight, **Ménière's disease**, **vestibular neuritis**, **labyrinthitis** and **positional vertigo** matter. In the cockpit, any of them adds to spatial disorientation (See M2V5).
A ICAO pede 1 a 3 meses sem voar, avalia: ICAO recommends 1 to 3 months without flying, specialist assessment and multi-crew flying for 2 years.

O **barotrauma do ouvido médio**, ou aer: **Middle ear barotrauma**, or aerotitis media, is injury caused by the difference between air pressure and middle ear pressure. It is the **most common ear disorder** among aircrew. It brings a **feeling of fullness**, **deafness**, **pain**, **tinnitus** and sometimes **vertigo**. The doctor grades the eardrum on the **Teed** scale, from grade **0**, symptoms only, to grade **5**, with **perforation**.
O **ruído** da cabine mascara a fala e,: Cabin **noise** masks speech and, over time, damages the ear (See M1V6 - II). Above **80 dB** there may be **temporary** loss: a 50 dB shift after 2 hours of exposure recovers in about **16 hours**, but a 60 dB shift takes days. Someone tested right after flying may have an audiogram **worse than the real one**. **Sudden** hearing loss in flight is rare.
O **tímpano** pode se romper por infecçã: The **eardrum** can rupture from infection, trauma or barotrauma. It usually heals, but the healed area is **thinner**; **atrophic areas** can rupture with a small pressure difference and are therefore treated as perforations. A simple perforation reduces hearing by about **10 to 15 dB**. **Cholesteatoma**, a mass of skin in the middle ear, can cause sudden vertigo and hearing loss.

O ouvido médio se comunica com o nariz p: The middle ear connects to the nose through the **auditory tube**, the Eustachian tube, which works as a **one-way valve**. On the **climb**, the air inside expands, forces the valve and leaves on its own, with a click. On the **descent**, outside pressure rises, the nasal end of the tube stays closed and air only gets in when the person **swallows**, **yawns**, **chews** or does the **Valsalva maneuver**. That is why the pain almost always comes **on descent**.
O ouvido médio, os **seios da face** e a: The middle ear, the **sinuses** and even a problem tooth hold **trapped air** in closed cavities. When outside pressure changes, this air expands or contracts (See M1V1 - II). The pressurized cabin stays between **5,000 and 8,000 ft**: at **564 mmHg**, at 8,000 ft, pressure is already about a quarter lower than the **760 mmHg** at sea level.

O ouvido também **ouve e equilibra**. A: The ear also **hears and balances**. The crew must understand the radio and colleagues amid cockpit noise, and the labyrinth reports the position of the head; sudden vertigo on descent can **incapacitate** the pilot (See M2V3 - III). For passengers, the pain usually passes without after-effects but can bring **dizziness**, **hearing loss**, **perforation** and **tinnitus**.

Pain coming from a blocked **maxillary sinus** mimics toothache (See M2V3 - V). A poorly sealed temporary filling can let air in under the skin.

Os **prazos depois do dentista**, sem do: The **waiting times after the dentist**, without pain, swelling or bleeding, are: **filling**, 24 hours, preferably 1 week; **simple extraction**, 24 to 48 hours; **uncomplicated implant**, **surgical extraction** and **root canal treatment**, 72 hours; **sinus lift** or **bone graft**, at least **2 weeks**. These times come mainly from experience with military crews.
Os **seios da face** são cavidades de ar: The **sinuses** are air cavities in the bones of the face: **frontal**, in the forehead; **maxillary**, in the cheeks; **ethmoid**, between the eyes; and **sphenoid**, at the back of the nose. They open into the nose through narrow channels. The nose also needs to work well to **ventilate** the sinuses and the tube and to **smell** smoke, oil or fuel.
